title: Under I/O pressure the agent stalls for minutes on a user action, silently
description:
Mark 2026-11-27: "nothing ever should hang, lock up, or go silent when
sent something to process. ever. thats always a bug. nobody tolerates
lag in a chat service" and "unexplaned random or long lag in a chat
service is a killing antifeature".

## What was found

`private_queries_are_one_to_one_rooms` (crates/mimid-agent/tests/irc_v2.rs)
PASSES in 349.61 seconds. Cargo even prints "has been running for over
60 seconds".

It was not slow before today because it could not be: the wait it sits
in had a 15 second deadline, so the test FAILED instead. Removing that
deadline (bead mimid-67e0) did not break anything; it replaced a random
failure with a measurement, and the measurement is 5.8 minutes.

The test configures `sync_interval_ms = 100`, so the periodic sync is
not the delay. Something in creating or observing a one-to-one room
takes minutes, and nothing in the path says why.

## Why this is P0

This is not a test problem. A private query is a user opening a direct
message, and the path under this test is the one a person waits on.
Minutes of silence after sending something to process is the
antifeature, and the flaky 15s deadline was hiding it: a test that fails
one run in fifteen reads as a flaky test, so nobody looks for the cause.

## What to do

1. Find where the time goes. The wait helpers now print what they are
   waiting for, so a timed run of this test with `--nocapture` says
   which wait holds and for how long. That run is in progress.
2. Fix the lag, not the test.
3. Then check the other long runs for the same thing. `jmap_seed` at
   13s and `push` at 11s are suspicious for the same reason, and the
   whole suite's 2224 tests took around 20 minutes with deadlines
   hiding whatever else is slow.

## The lesson for the rest of the sweep

Every deadline removed in bead mimid-67e0 may uncover one of these. That
is the point rather than a cost: a guessed timeout converts a latency
bug into an intermittent failure, which is the form in which it gets
ignored.

## Timed run, 2026-11-27

The wait helpers' own output, timestamped. Test ran 00:18:57 to 00:25:23.

  00:18:57  test starts
  00:22:14  first "waiting for a line from the server"   <- 3m17s gap
  00:22:19  ten lines exchanged in five seconds
  00:24:23  the next line, at "seen 10"                  <- 2m04s gap
  00:24:28  16s gap, then 14s, then 18s
  00:25:19  "waiting for the daemon to stop"
  00:25:23  passes

## Why it finishes at all, rather than failing

`Irc::until` reads lines until one matches, and the IRC front end sends
PING after 90 seconds of silence (DEFAULT_PING_AFTER, lib.rs:145). So a
keepalive hands the reader a line, it does not match, and the wait goes
round again. The 2m04s gap is about two keepalive periods. That is why
removing the 15s deadline turned a failure into a slow pass instead of a
hang.

## What the gaps are around

The test registers alice and bob on the SAME provider, then alice sends
the first PRIVMSG to bob, which creates a one-to-one room. So the slow
step is opening a direct message with someone for the first time: MLS
group creation, the KeyPackage fetch and the Welcome, any of which could
be sitting on a retry.

A person opening a DM waits on exactly this path. Minutes is the
antifeature.

## Next

A debug-level run of the same test is in progress to name the step that
holds. Until it lands this bead says where the time is, not yet why.

## Correction, 2026-11-27: it is intermittent, not always

A third run of the same test finished in 11.77 seconds, with every wait
logged inside a four second window and no gap at all. So the earlier
claim here -- that this path takes minutes -- is wrong as stated. The
three runs were 349.61s, 375.65s and 11.77s.

What the slow runs had in common: both followed a `cargo clean`, so a
full rebuild ran first and the page cache was cold, and the filesystem
had just had 178 GiB freed.

That points at the same thing the original gate failure showed, which
was a SQLite `PRAGMA journal_mode = WAL` taking 2.414809295 seconds --
a statement that should be microseconds. Under I/O pressure the agent's
database work goes orders of magnitude slower, and this path does enough
of it to stall for minutes.

## So the bug, restated

Not "opening a DM takes minutes". It is: under I/O pressure the agent
stalls for minutes on a user action, with nothing logged to say what it
is waiting for. A person would see a chat client go silent after sending
the first message to someone, with no indication whether it failed.

Dropping P0 to P1. The lag is real and reproducible under load, but it
is not the unconditional six minutes this bead first claimed, and the
difference matters for anyone who picks it up.

## What is still worth doing

1. The agent logs nothing across a multi-minute stall. The test harness
   installs no tracing subscriber, so the in-process daemon's own
   logging goes nowhere, which is why this took three runs to
   characterise. Both halves are worth fixing: the daemon should say
   what it is waiting on, and the harness should capture it.
2. Find what the path does enough of to be that sensitive to I/O. A
   first DM creates a one-to-one room: MLS group creation, a KeyPackage
   fetch, a Welcome. If any step writes and fsyncs per message rather
   than per batch, that is the multiplier.
3. The 2.4s PRAGMA deserves its own look. WAL mode is set per
   connection; if the agent opens connections per operation rather than
   pooling, every one pays that.
notes:
2026-11-27: the three remaining actions are now beads mimid-604m.1 (no tracing subscriber in the harness, nothing logged across the stall), mimid-604m.2 (what the first-DM path does that makes it I/O-sensitive by 30x), mimid-604m.3 (the 2.4s PRAGMA and connection pooling). .2 is blocked on .1.
2026-11-27, bead mimid-c90r landed: mimid-agent now has the JSON log format and an OTLP export, so its events can be queried and alerted on. What this bead still wants is a span: the agent opens none, so `[telemetry] traces` exports nothing. A span per sync turn, with the turn's outcome, is what would show a stall as a duration rather than as a test that takes 5.8 minutes. The agent's Limitations in crates/mimid-agent/src/lib.rs point here for it.
2026-11-27, a second and much smaller reproduction, found while testing the agent binary's log (crates/mimid-agent/tests/binary_log.rs). One provider, one agent, no rooms, no IRC, no messages. Idle machine: 1.7 s. Immediately after a workspace build, with the disk busy: 149.6 s. Timed by phase during one loaded run: tests/common's server() -- open the provider's SQLite and run its migrations -- took 29.98 s; the agent's first log line came 7 ms later; from there to a clean exit, which includes Daemon::start publishing KeyPackages to that provider, 12.24 s. Nothing in those phases waits on the network: both ends are loopback in or beside the test process. The common factor across both reproductions is SQLite under I/O pressure, which points at the journal and synchronous settings of the two stores rather than at the sync loop.
SPANS AND A HARNESS, 2026-11-27, Mark: "do all three, spans first".

THE SPANS. A message now has a span at each hop it takes, all at DEBUG so [telemetry] span_level exports them without the terminal log printing them:

- the sender's store: store_send (user, room, files, msgid)
- the sender's agent: agent_send_content (room, silent, msgid), and under it mls_encrypt_and_stage and provider_submit, which is the split the question needed: MLS plus two SQLite writes on one side, the network call on the other
- the sender's provider: fanout_attempt (room_id, domain, id, fanout_seq, attempts)
- the receiving provider: store_fanout (room_id, from, fanout_seq, messages)
- the receiving store: store_sync (user, messages, joined, problems) and store_received (room, msgid, sent_here)
- the receiving agent: agent_receive (fetched), and under it finish_outbox, provider_fetch and handle_message (message)

msgid is the message ID as lowercase hex, the rendering a record, an IRC msgid tag and a JMAP senderMsgId already use, so the two agents' halves join on it. The providers carry no msgid and cannot: a FanoutMessage is a timestamp and an MLSMessage, and the ID is inside the ciphertext, so the middle of the path joins on the room and the fanout sequence.

THE HARNESS. crates/mimid-agent/tests/message_path.rs starts two providers, peers of each other, a daemon on each, and a JMAP client for each, sends one message from alice to bob and prints the hops with the time each took. It reads the spans back in process through mimid_telemetry::timeline, not from the log: a span carrying no event appears in no log however long it took, and a span is the only place a hop's duration is recorded at all.

Both daemons run with sync_interval_ms = 3600000, so no arrival can be a poll's doing. That is the one timing assertion here that does not depend on the machine, since it is a configuration and not a deadline. The budget on the whole path is 60 s, far above what it costs, so what fails is a stall and not a slow machine; the failure prints the table.

MEASURED on an idle machine, a message across two providers: 78 ms end to end.

  store_send             1.803210765s   42.729862ms
  mls_encrypt_and_stage  1.803429555s    9.323760ms
  provider_submit        1.812766257s   20.921821ms
  fanout_attempt         1.819919145s   15.387531ms
  store_fanout           1.819940712s    8.975589ms
  agent_receive          1.853460943s   28.965610ms
  provider_fetch         1.853555548s    4.896244ms
  store_received         1.880863822s  125.428000us

NEXT, and this is still open. The 349 second run that started this bead was private_queries_are_one_to_one_rooms (crates/mimid-agent/tests/irc_v2.rs), an IRC path on one provider. The tooling to measure it now exists; the measurement has not been taken. The IRC front end has no spans, so a trace of it starts at the store: an IRC command's own work is still invisible. mimid-604m.2 (the write and fsync count) and mimid-604m.3 (the 2.4 s pragma) are untouched.
BOTH NAMED CAUSES FIXED, 2026-11-27. The bead stays open for its two remaining children.

Cause one, and nobody had guessed it: `Agent::host_room` built a new MLS group, its first Commit and the merge with no transaction open. OpenMLS writes each piece of a new group as it goes, and a write with no transaction open is a transaction of its own, so building one room cost 28 write transactions -- 28 of the sender's 36 for one first private message, 112 of its 145 fsyncs, all under the agent mutex. `build_commit`, `join` and `join_external` all already wrapped this work in `Agent::in_transaction`; `host_room` was the one path that did not. One transaction takes it to 4 (commit 187ff0d3). The test counts rows rather than seconds: a fail point between the group and its first Commit, row counts read on a second connection, and it fails on the old code at 22 rows against 10.

Cause two: the agent's database ran in SQLite's rollback-journal mode at four fsyncs a commit, while the server's store had been in WAL all along. It now runs in a write-ahead log (decision mimid-1wgh.134, commit 99ddbc9c): 192 fsyncs to 49 for one first DM, journal creates and directory fsyncs to zero, the client's echo 35.8 s to 11.2 s under a 279 ms mean fsync. The cost is that `secure_delete` became eventual, which `chat_delete`'s rewritten test now states and proves in both directions.

THE MUTEX IS NOT THE BUG, and was left alone with the invariant written down: `Store::host` must hold the agent across `host_room` and every `invite`, because `Store::sync`'s `reconcile_rooms` records any room the agent is active in, so a window between them gives one room two records, and an invite that then fails makes `Store::host` report no room where a record already exists. The critical section's shape was right; its length was not.

Supporting beads: mimid-604m.1 the subscriber that made measuring possible, mimid-604m.2 the measurement, mimid-604m.3 the pooling defect, mimid-604m.4 and mimid-604m.5 the journal mode, mimid-604m.6 this fix.
